presentingComplaint: Six weeks of fatigue, mild aching in the hands and wrists, and 'frothy' urine noticed by her husband; no rash.
history: 58-year-old woman with a 2-year history of vague joint aches previously attributed to osteoarthritis, and a single episode of unexplained thrombocytopenia 4 years ago. Over the past 6 weeks she reports increasing tiredness, poor appetite with ~4 kg unintentional weight loss, and low-grade evening temperatures she attributed to the menopause. She has noticed mild ankle swelling and persistently frothy urine. She denies a facial rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, or Raynaud phenomenon - hence the presentation was initially thought to be 'age-related' and non-specific. No recent infection, no new drugs, no NSAID overuse. This is a late-onset, pauci-symptomatic flare dominated by renal and haematological features rather than the classic malar-rash / acute polyarthritis picture.
examination: Comfortable, not toxic. No malar or discoid rash, no oral ulcers. Mild symmetrical synovitis of the 2nd/3rd MCPs and wrists with no deformity. Bilateral pitting pedal oedema to mid-shin. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Cardiorespiratory exam unremarkable; no rub. BP mildly elevated.

labs.urinalysis: protein 3+, blood 2+, dysmorphic RBCs with occasional RBC casts

imaging: Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys with preserved cortico-medullary differentiation, no obstruction. CXR clear, no effusion.
microbiology: Blood cultures negative; urine culture no growth; hepatitis B/C and HIV serology negative (pre-immunosuppression screen).
finalDiagnosis: SLE flare with proliferative lupus nephritis and autoimmune cytopenias (late-onset, atypical constitutional/renal-dominant presentation)
citations: EULAR - Recommendations for the management of SLE - 2023
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
stewardship: Non-infective autoimmune flare; no empirical antibiotics indicated. Exclude infection (cultures, viral screen) before immunosuppression; ensure vaccination and PJP prophylaxis consideration once high-dose steroids/cyclophosphamide or MMF started.
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, iodinated contrast) given active nephritis
Screen and treat latent infection (HBV/HCV/HIV/TB) before immunosuppression
edgeCases: Late-onset SLE (>50y) is frequently misattributed to malignancy, infection or degenerative disease due to prominent constitutional and serositis features and fewer cutaneous signs
Normal/near-normal CRP with high ESR helps distinguish active lupus from intercurrent infection
Low C3/C4 with high anti-dsDNA supports renal flare over TMA or ANCA vasculitis
expectedMaiK: Recognise a serologically-active SLE flare with proliferative lupus nephritis and autoimmune cytopenias despite the absence of classic mucocutaneous features; confirm with anti-dsDNA/complement and proceed to renal biopsy for ISN/RPS class, then induction immunosuppression (glucocorticoids plus MMF or cyclophosphamide, with hydroxychloroquine as backbone).

Peripheral smear, haptoglobin, LDH, reticulocytes and direct Coombs to characterise cytopenias
